channel.title: AI.DOG Learning & Portfolio Library
channel.description: Evidence-led notes for learning AI and building inspectable portfolio work.

item.title: Thinking about AI engineering? Start with what the role needs you to deliver
item.description: Do not chase a title first. See who receives the work, then work backwards to the portfolio piece you need.

item.title: What should you add before putting a RAG chatbot in your portfolio?
item.description: State the user problem, where the data comes from, how answers are checked, what happens when they are wrong, and what you actually built.

item.title: From a vague request to an AI feature someone can check
item.description: Turn “add AI” into a clear task, checks, a record of fixes, and human review.

item.title: After changing a prompt, leave a record someone can check
item.description: Record the prompt version, fixed tests, allowed permissions, failure handling, and human approval.

item.title: How to judge whether an AI course, hackathon or event is worth it
item.description: Score opportunities by role relevance, tangible output, time cost, eligibility and reusable evidence.

item.title: AI Engineer interviews: what should you practise first?
item.description: Choose one question from ten capability areas, answer it first, then add the mechanism, trade-off, failure case, and a project you can talk through.

item.title: Turn a RAG idea into a PolicyPilot someone can review
item.description: A fictional policy-support assistant that separates its implemented keyword baseline, cited draft, and human handoff from a later RAG/model-evaluation extension that needs separate approval.

item.title: Renewal Triage: use a past snapshot to order a human-review queue
item.description: Use fully synthetic renewal data to practise time-safe inputs, a first rule, capacity-aware routing, change checks, and when to return to the earlier method.

item.title: Turn a course exercise into portfolio work you can explain
item.description: Do not copy the tutorial. Say what it taught, what you changed, how you compared approaches, where it failed, and which work was yours.

item.title: How do you check an AI automation without writing code?
item.description: Choose one low-risk task, have AI produce a draft, check it with a few fixed cases, and leave the final decision to a person.

item.title: How to review a coding-agent AI demo when you do not write code
item.description: Review the plan, acceptance cases, diff, permissions and reviewer decision first; keep GitHub evidence, not a one-line “done” claim.

item.title: Six questions to ask before putting an AI portfolio on GitHub
item.description: Look at what the system does, whether its data may be used, what you tested, and who takes over when it fails. Then choose one thing to improve.

item.title: Eight weeks: turn one AI course into a project you can explain
item.description: Start with one capability you need to build, then leave a fictional case, checks, limits, and a README.

item.title: Decide what you will make before choosing an AI course
item.description: Start with a gap, then check that the course gives you a practical task, usable feedback, and a next step to record.

item.title: AI Engineer Interview Quick Start: 16 practice cards
item.description: These 16 cards are a quick start, not the whole question bank. Each links to one standalone practice question; the full Interview Lab has 59 practice questions across ten capability routes.

item.title: Use AI without writing code: turn a prompt into a workflow
item.description: You do not need model internals first. Choose one low-risk task, have AI produce a draft, check fixed cases, and leave the decision to a person.

item.title: Before you click Allow: a non-coder's first AI-agent permission review
item.description: Use a fictional career evidence-gap matrix to review file, network, account and external-action requests—then retain a human approval and inspectable receipt.

item.title: Use AI as a coding partner: keep the scope, tests and reviewer decision
item.description: AI can propose a plan, diff and tests. You and the reviewer still own feature boundaries, data permissions, acceptance and the decision to accept or stop.

item.title: Use AI as a coder: build a resumable batch worker without duplicates or runaway spend
item.description: Use synthetic work items to practise a serial queue, retries, terminal idempotency, checkpoints and dead-letter review; it keeps human-review records only and takes no real document action.

item.title: Approval Queue: keep FAQ drafts before human approval
item.description: Use a fully synthetic FAQ queue to show the work boundary, transparent first rule, fixed safety cases, a non-executing gpt-5-mini fixture, traces, and a reviewer gate.

item.title: AI engineer interviews: why a higher model score may not mean a better decision
item.description: Move from F1, thresholds and calibration to reviewer capacity, shadow mode and release gates—without mistaking a higher score for business value.

item.title: AI engineer interviews: why a good agent answer can still be a failed workflow
item.description: Do not judge an agent from its final reply alone. Check what tools it tried to use, how it stopped, what it recorded, how retries behave, and when a person must take over.

item.title: Before GitHub: say what each portfolio file is for
item.description: Do not stop at code and screenshots. Explain the decision, data limits, comparison, tests, human-review point, and what the work cannot claim.

item.title: From local tests to an authorised trial: how to measure an AI workflow
item.description: Keep model scores, workflow observations, and still-unknown outcomes separate. State who decides, what data is allowed, what you compare, and when to stop.

item.title: Choose an AI learning source by role and evidence gap: four starting routes
item.description: Not a course ranking: choose a route from your target role and prerequisite, then keep a first-week record of how the system works and where it may be used.

item.title: AI engineering shared language: from one model call to a deliverable system
item.description: Use a bounded policy-draft flow to separate an LLM, context, RAG, MCP, an agent, quantization, and the person who can actually decide.

item.title: Transformers, generation, and fine-tuning: move from mechanism to trade-off
item.description: Use one fixed task to understand attention, decoding, context budgets, and model architecture before choosing a prompt, retrieval, workflow, or training change.

item.title: Before you tune: understand how a model learns from error
item.description: Use a small synthetic classification task to understand representations, loss, gradients, backpropagation, validation, and signals of overfitting.

item.title: From an AI request to an accepted change: implementation evidence is more than code that runs
item.description: Use one small synthetic feature to practise an input contract, negative cases, tests, diff review and a reviewer decision.

item.title: Stoppable AI agents and P99 serving: from tool contracts to human handoff
item.description: Use a synthetic, draft-only case to connect agent state, retries, traces, prefill/decode, and serving budgets—without confusing speed with reliability.

item.title: A multimodal demo people can review
item.description: Use a fictional image, document, and speech workflow to separate quality, wait time, privacy, fallback, and human handoff.

item.title: Read frontier AI claims with source receipts, not hype
item.description: Turn papers and model releases into claims, baselines, methods, limits, and traceable decisions.

item.title: Build a reviewable AI packet from public vulnerability data
item.description: Use public KEV data to record the source and allowed use, then compare a change against fixed cases. If a required case fails, a person decides whether to hold or roll it back. Do not scan, patch, or claim organisational exposure.

item.title: Before choosing a learning mode: write the decision and baseline
item.description: Start with available evidence, an observation cutoff, and a human decision to separate supervised learning, exploratory analysis, and an honest first baseline.

item.title: Linear and logistic models: move from an output number to a human decision
item.description: Separate continuous estimates, classification probabilities, feature availability, thresholds, and human handoff instead of treating one score as an automatic decision.

item.title: A lower loss is not a better decision: test regularisation and generalisation
item.description: Separate training loss, validation, regularisation, error cost, and workflow result so a tidy curve does not become a product claim.

item.title: Gradients and backpropagation: where to start when a loss curve fails
item.description: Trace one prediction to a parameter update, then use tiny-batch tests, input checks, and training logs to diagnose NaNs, flat loss, and false improvement.

item.title: Why training is unstable: dropout, normalisation, and reproducible experiments
item.description: Separate data, seed, split, and optimiser problems before comparing dropout, normalisation, learning rates, and batch-size trade-offs.

item.title: Do you actually need a sequence model? From event order to framework boundaries
item.description: Write the observation cutoff, tabular baseline, and allowed decision before comparing RNNs, LSTMs, GRUs, attention, and framework trade-offs.

item.title: Tokenisation and domain terms: audit the input before saying a model does not understand
item.description: Use token counts, near-match codes, structured fields, and contrast cases to separate representation, retrieval, and workflow problems.

item.title: Attention Q, K, V, masks, and position: explain them with one order-sensitive case
item.description: Go beyond the equation by using fixed inputs, a future-token boundary, and negative cases to test order, negation, and forbidden context.

item.title: Transformer blocks and architecture choice: begin with the task contract, not the model name
item.description: Use a small routing-plus-grounded-draft flow to distinguish encoder, decoder, attention blocks, output contracts, and workflow boundaries.

item.title: A decoding strategy is not a personality: use an output policy instead of blindly tuning temperature
item.description: Put temperature, sampling, schema, citations, fixed cases, and handoff into an acceptance flow instead of trusting one fluent output.

item.title: Long context may still miss the middle: retrieval, lost-middle failures, and evidence coverage
item.description: Use fixed long-document cases to test whether the system cites, abstains, or hands off when relevant evidence appears at the beginning, middle, end, or beside a conflict.

item.title: Modern attention, MoE, and serving: move from a model label back to workload and budget
item.description: Put context length, sparse experts, prefill, decode, batching, and P99 back into a fixed workload, with unknowns, fallback, and a stop condition.

item.title: Which language-model family fits the task? Start with four jobs, not a leaderboard
item.description: Separate classification, retrieval, drafting, and image reading; connect them to task, error cost, evaluation, and human handoff before selecting a model.

item.title: The model is wrong. Do you really need fine-tuning? From data and alignment to a decision record
item.description: Separate stale knowledge, input contracts, label problems, and repeatable transformations before using a baseline, lawful data, evaluation, and rollback to judge adaptation.

item.title: Prompts, context compaction, and multilingual evals: longer is not automatically better
item.description: Version instructions, evidence, history, and output contracts separately, then test English, Cantonese, code-switching, and long-thread cases for grounding, schema, and handoff.

item.title: RAG index, chunks, reranking, and cache: every layer can find the wrong evidence
item.description: Use one correct clause, a tempting FAQ, an old version, and a no-answer case to separate metadata, chunk size, reranking, cache, and permission trade-offs.

item.title: When RAG sources are stale or conflict: citations need authority and handoff
item.description: Put effective dates, scope, owner, replacement, and authority into a source policy; make conflicting evidence detectable, abstainable, and human-reviewable.

item.title: Agent memory, planning, and reflection: remembering more is not more reliable
item.description: Separate run state, retrieved knowledge, durable memory, and tool authority; test an agent with stale-memory, budget, out-of-scope, and handoff cases.

item.title: AI hardware, routing, deployment, and transport: from a request contract to a stoppable flow
item.description: Do not start with a GPU catalogue. Define input routes, deterministic stops, CPU/accelerator/memory/queue/network trade-offs, budgets, and human handoff first.

item.title: World models and self-improvement: narrow a frontier claim into inspectable state, eval, and release gates
item.description: Use a fully fictional triage simulator to separate state transitions, candidate updates, an evaluator, human approval, and rollback instead of treating self-improvement as deployable capability.

item.title: Agent protocols, orchestration, and computer use: capability is not permission
item.description: Use a read-only-fixture-to-review-packet flow to separate protocols, orchestrators, computer use, action contracts, and human approval.

item.title: AI harnesses and completion criteria: decide how to check before choosing a framework
item.description: Write down the input, source, output format, route, time limit, record, checks, and reviewer. Do not call a fluent paragraph complete on its own.

item.title: Inference, memory, scheduling, and serving engines: break down the request path before blaming P99
item.description: Use a fixed synthetic workload to separate queue, prefill, decode, tools, validation, retries, memory, batching, and fallback instead of using one average to explain everything.

item.title: LLM evals, human review, and observability: a fluent answer is not enough to release
item.description: A fluent answer is not enough. Check each fixed case, have a person review errors, keep a before-and-after record for every change, and stop if a required case fails. A passing local check is not production approval.

item.title: Write safety in from the first step: data, actions, owners, and stop points
item.description: Use a risk register, data/action boundaries, detection, owners, safe stops, and synthetic failure cases to write safety into the flow.

item.title: A multimodal document flow: from image input to human review
item.description: Separate acquisition, extraction, comparison, generation, and action; test against an OCR-plus-review baseline with visual ambiguity, injection, privacy, and handoff cases.

item.title: Five official starting points for agent and eval learning
item.description: Choose an official starting point for agent fundamentals, state, runtime events, Promptfoo cases, or cloud evaluation, with checked prerequisites, a Week-1 exercise, feedback route, and limits.

item.title: Use source material to write a context brief for human review
item.description: Use invented, synthetic monthly values laid out like the public series. Practise keeping a source record, rejecting unsuitable material, checking fixed cases, and preparing a context brief for human review—without forecasting a labour market.

item.title: Build one flagship AI portfolio case first: six rows a reviewer can inspect
item.description: Use one synthetic or public-data case to record an artefact, a check, and a nonclaim in each row. Start a second project only when it adds a genuinely different decision.
